Title: [from] The Inca Chasqui
Author: by Wendi Silvano
Content: Every boy, when he reached the age of `text(fourteen)`, was expected to train for service in the Inca empire. To pay his mita, or tax `ultext(requirement)`, each was assigned a particular service. Some were chosen to be builders or soldiers. Others were servants in the Sapa Inca’s¹ household. The fastest and most dependable boys were chosen to be Chasquis.
Chasquis were stationed in small, `text(one-room)` huts about every `text(two miles)` along the rock-paved Inca road system.

`text(Each boy)` carried a message or parcel as fast as he could to the next hut and passed it on to a waiting runner. In this manner, messages could traverse the entire Inca kingdom, from north to south, in just a matter of `text(days)`. Chasquis had to be strong, loyal, and brave. If even `text(one)` runner failed to make his delivery, the entire chain would be broken, and the message would never reach its destination.

Natu heard the wail of the conch shell, signaling an approaching runner . He scurried up the hill to where his older brother Mayta stood ready. Mayta was the fastest Chasqui in the southeast quarter. Natu loved to see him run.
He watched with envy as Muru, the runner, told Mayta the message. Then, like a racing puma, Mayta sped off toward the next hut.
Muru stood, looking majestic in his white headdress, his club and sling carefully tucked in the pouch at his side. Natu smiled.
“Can you tell me today?” he asked Muru.
“Yes, Natu. Today we carry word to the Sapa Inca that the northwest quarter has had an earthquake and needs supplies and men. Tomorrow the governor will send a quipu² detailing just what he requires.
“Then I will see you tomorrow?” said Natu.
“I suppose you will,” replied Muru.
“Good.”

For `text(three years)` Natu had watched Mayta and Muru with admiration. For `text(three years)` he had longed for the `text(day)` when it would be he who raced along this rugged stretch on the road to the Inca capital of Cuzco.
“Tell me of today’s journey,” begged Natu the moment Mayta appeared in the doorway that evening.
“All right,” said Mayta. “Just give me a moment to catch my breath.”
Natu sat by him on the llama-skin mat that was his bed.

“Today was quite exciting. I had only just started up the steep slope when our friend, the puma, decided it liked the smell of the guinea pig Mother had given me for lunch. It glared at me with a look so fierce that I wondered if maybe it wasn’t thinking how much more meat there would be on a Chasqui!”
Natu laughed. “What did you do?”

“For a few moments we both stood frozen, staring at each other like `text(two)` llamas eyeing the same patch of grass. I carefully reached into my pouch and pulled out my sling and the meat. I slid the meat into the sling and pulled it back as slowly as I could. Then, with a shout that echoed over the mountain and back again, I shot that meat right past our friend’s nose and so deep into the brush that I’m sure it took the puma quite some time to find it. ”
“Oh, Mayta!” said Natu, beaming with pride. “You are so cunning and brave. I, too, wish for such adventure!”

Natu arose early the next morning. He wanted to take the llamas to pasture at dawn so he wouldn’t miss Muru’s arrival. He listened to every sound that swept down through the mountain passes, expecting to hear the blow of a conch. What he heard instead made him tighten with fear . It was Mayta’s voice yelling for help!
Natu ran up the slope, where he found his brother Mayta lying on the ground, writhing and grabbing his ankle.
“Mayta!” yelled Natu. “Are you all right?”
“Oh, Natu,” grunted Mayta. “I fear I have lost a battle with a lowly stone. ”
Mayta winced with pain as Natu helped him up. Slowly they made their way to the hut, where Mayta rested on the mat. They both looked down at his swollen ankle.
“Just wait until Muru sees this,” said Mayta. “The tale will reach Cuzco faster than any message ever sent to the Sapa Inca.”
Natu didn’t know whether to laugh or cry. But he knew there was not time for either. In the distance he could hear the sound of the conch. Muru was coming!
“Natu,” cried Mayta. “You must take the quipu. I cannot run.”
“But, Mayta —”
“No buts. The chain must not be broken. Muru will be too tired to go on. You know the route. You can do it.”
Natu’s heart pounded. This was the chance he had always hoped for — the chance to prove he could be a Chasqui.
“I will do it, my brother. I won’t let you down.”
He grabbed Mayta’s headdress and pouch.
“Mayta is hurt!” called Natu as Muru neared. “Pass me the quipu and go help him. ”
Muru hesitated just a moment. He looked at Natu, then at the hut. “Here, ” he said. “Be careful.”
